Rural or outer island resident without connection: Lives on a more remote island or rural area where grid access is limited or unreliable, and does not have a stable electric connection to their home.

Young adult in shared or informal housing: Rents a room or lives in informal accommodation where electricity may be shared or not formally connected in their name, creating some uncertainty about their status.

Elderly or low-income resident uncertain about details: Older or economically disadvantaged person who may have electricity but is unsure of the technical details of their connection, or who relies on others to manage household utilities.
Urban middle-class professional with regular internet use and electricity access who has a stable salaried job or business income, rarely going without cash income even during difficult times.
Urban resident with irregular employment or informal sector work who experiences occasional cash shortfalls, going without income just once or twice in the past year during slow periods.

Rural household member without electricity and relying on water outside the compound, engaged in subsistence farming or casual labor, frequently going without reliable cash income several times a year.
Vulnerable urban or peri-urban resident living in poverty with no stable income source, going without cash income many times or almost always, struggling to meet basic needs consistently.
Household member in a slightly better-off rural or small-town setting with some access to remittances or small trade, who occasionally faces cash shortages but manages to get by most of the time.
Urban middle-class professional who personally owns a motorcycle or car as a primary means of transportation for work and daily life in cities like Praia or Mindelo.
Household member who relies on a vehicle owned by another family member, such as a spouse or parent, and does not personally own one but benefits from household access.
Rural or lower-income resident who cannot afford a motor vehicle or motorcycle and relies on public transport or walking, with no household member owning one either.
Young adult or secondary earner in the household who has steady cash income but has not yet invested in a personal vehicle, though another household member owns one.
Established household head with stable income who owns a vehicle primarily for family use and considers it an important asset given Cabo Verde's island geography and limited public transport.
Urban young professional or student living in a city apartment or shared housing who has piped water connected directly inside their house or flat, making indoor water access the norm for them.
Resident of a peri-urban or suburban compound where the household shares a communal tap or water point within the compound walls, which is the most common setup in Kenyan towns and estates.
Rural youth living in a village or small town where the nearest water source — a borehole, communal tap, or river — is located outside the compound, requiring them to fetch water from a distance.
Young person in an informal settlement or slum area where water access is irregular and typically sourced from a shared kiosk or vendor outside the compound, reflecting urban poverty conditions.
Young person in a well-established middle-class urban home with full indoor plumbing and reliable piped water supply directly inside the house, representing a more privileged minority.

Young urban residents who were skeptical of the COVID-19 vaccine due to distrust of government and foreign institutions, and who largely avoided vaccination, reflecting the low reported COVID illness rates suggesting limited engagement with the health system overall.

Middle-aged household heads who were cautious about the vaccine due to rumors and misinformation circulating in their communities, and who chose not to get vaccinated despite some awareness of the pandemic.

Community-minded individuals who followed official health guidance and got vaccinated, either through workplace requirements or local health campaigns, seeing vaccination as a responsible choice for their family.

Older or rural residents with limited access to vaccination centers and little interaction with formal health services, who did not receive the vaccine primarily due to logistical barriers rather than strong opposition.
Individuals who are genuinely uncertain about their vaccination status or who received a dose but are unsure whether it counted as a full course, reflecting confusion about the vaccination process.

A rural villager with strong community ties who is generally open to people of different ethnicities as neighbours, reflecting the relatively tolerant attitude toward ethnic diversity seen in Benin's multi-ethnic society. They would not particularly care about having neighbours from other ethnic groups.
A traditional community elder who somewhat dislikes the idea of neighbours from other ethnic groups, preferring to live among familiar people from their own community and fearing cultural disruption.
A younger person from a market town who has had regular contact with traders and people from various ethnic backgrounds, and who actually welcomes or likes having neighbours from other ethnic groups.
A person with strong ethnic identity who strongly dislikes the idea of neighbours from other ethnic groups, viewing them with suspicion or as a threat to local customs and land rights.
An older person who is uncertain or indifferent, having little strong opinion either way but leaning slightly toward discomfort with unfamiliar ethnic groups due to limited exposure.
Family-oriented urban Namibians who place deep trust in their relatives, viewing family bonds as the foundation of social life and a reliable support network in times of need.
Pragmatic urban residents who trust their relatives quite a lot but acknowledge that family relationships can be complicated, maintaining strong but not unconditional trust.
Moderately trusting individuals who have had mixed experiences with relatives, perhaps due to financial disputes or family tensions, and therefore trust them only somewhat.
Cautious urban dwellers who have experienced betrayal or disappointment from family members and extend only a little trust to relatives, preferring to rely on themselves or close friends.
Deeply distrustful individuals who have been significantly let down by relatives and place virtually no trust in them, viewing family ties as unreliable or even harmful.

Rural subsistence farmers with limited access to healthcare and testing who never received an official COVID-19 diagnosis, and thus report no household member was ill or tested positive, even if some family members experienced respiratory illness.

Urban or peri-urban residents with slightly more access to clinics or information who had at least one household member fall ill with COVID-19 symptoms or receive a positive test, and acknowledge the household was affected.

People who are uncertain whether their household's illness was COVID-19 or another disease, given limited testing availability in Madagascar, and lean toward saying no simply because they never had a confirmed test.
Individuals who lost income and faced hardship during the pandemic but whose household members did not personally fall ill with COVID-19, and clearly report no illness in the household.
People who are reluctant to discuss health matters or distrust the framing of the question, either refusing to answer or expressing genuine uncertainty about whether their household was affected.

Urban, internet-connected Angolans who follow news and international affairs and are aware of some foreign aid relationships, but are uncertain about Japan specifically and likely to say they don't know.
Rural or less educated Angolans with limited internet access and little exposure to international development news, who have no knowledge of Japan's assistance and will say they don't know.

Angolans who are aware of China's dominant presence in Angolan development and infrastructure, and may confuse or conflate Asian donor countries, leading them to guess 'Yes' for Japan even with limited specific knowledge.

Angolans with some exposure to government communications or civil society organizations who have genuinely heard about Japanese development assistance or JICA projects in Angola and confidently answer 'Yes'.

Skeptical or disengaged Angolans who, given their frustration with government handling of corruption and economic hardship, distrust foreign aid narratives and are inclined to say 'No' or that they haven't heard enough.
Middle-aged wage earner in a stable job who manages household expenses adequately, feeling they are coping but not thriving on their income, with little financial cushion for unexpected costs.
Pensioner or older married couple living on retirement income, finding it increasingly difficult to cover rising costs of living on a fixed pension.
Dual-income married household where both spouses work, allowing them to live comfortably and cover expenses without significant financial stress.
Working-class married person in a lower-wage job or with irregular employment, struggling to make ends meet and finding their income very difficult to live on.

Self-employed or small business owner whose income fluctuates, sometimes comfortable but often uncertain, generally describing their situation as difficult depending on the season or economic conditions.
Secular, liberal villagers who value personal freedom and have no strong religious objections to homosexuality; they strongly support gay men and lesbians living as they wish.

Moderately religious Catholics who may personally disapprove of homosexuality but still believe in individual freedom and non-interference in others' private lives; they tend to agree that gay people should be free to live as they wish.

Traditionally religious villagers with conservative Catholic values who feel uncomfortable with homosexuality and are reluctant to fully endorse gay people's freedom to live openly as they wish, though they may not actively oppose it.

Strongly conservative or devoutly religious individuals who believe homosexuality conflicts with their moral or religious values and disagree that gay men and lesbians should be free to live as they wish.
Younger or more educated villagers who are broadly tolerant and strongly affirm the right of gay men and lesbians to live freely, seeing it as a basic matter of human rights and equality.

Traditional Jewish Israelis who married young and followed conventional religious or cultural norms, never cohabiting before marriage. They view living together outside marriage as contrary to their values and have never done so.
Secular or moderately traditional Israelis who cohabited with a partner at some point before marriage, viewing it as a practical or romantic step that was common in their social circles.
Arab Israeli citizens who adhere to conservative Muslim or Christian family values, having followed traditional paths of marriage without prior cohabitation.
Haredi or religiously observant Jewish Israelis for whom cohabitation outside marriage is strictly forbidden by religious law, and who have never lived with a partner without being married.

More liberal or secular Israelis who cohabited with a partner for an extended period, possibly never marrying, reflecting a broader acceptance of alternative family arrangements that grew in Israel from the 1980s onward.

Pragmatic moderates who broadly accept cohabitation and non-traditional family arrangements, seeing having a child with an unmarried partner as a normal and acceptable life choice in modern Czech society.
Liberal approvers who strongly support individual freedom in family formation and view marriage as unnecessary for raising children, enthusiastically approving of this arrangement.
Neutral observers who neither approve nor disapprove, feeling it is a personal matter that does not concern them, though they may have mild reservations about the lack of legal commitment.

Traditional-leaning individuals who prefer marriage before having children and mildly disapprove of this arrangement, feeling it provides less stability for the child even if they accept cohabitation itself.

Strongly traditional people, often older or more religious, who disapprove or strongly disapprove of having children outside of marriage, seeing it as undermining family values and the child's wellbeing.

Older working-class individuals who were part of the strong Belgian trade union tradition during their working years but have since retired or left the workforce, and thus were previously members of a union.
Current workers in sectors with strong union presence (manufacturing, public sector, retail) who are active union members and see it as a natural part of working life in Belgium.
People who have never joined a union, often working in smaller businesses, part-time, or informal arrangements where union membership felt irrelevant or inaccessible to them.
Individuals who were briefly union members at some point but let their membership lapse, perhaps due to changing jobs, disillusionment, or feeling the union did not represent their interests well.
Younger or less-educated workers who are employed in precarious or low-wage jobs and have never been approached by or felt connected to a union, seeing it as something for others.

Older working-class or retired individuals who worked in manufacturing, public sector, or traditional industries where union membership was common and expected; they were members in the past but have since retired or left those sectors.
Middle-aged or older adults who have never joined a union, working in small private businesses, agriculture, or self-employment typical of Italian small towns where union culture is less prevalent.
Current union members, often public sector workers such as teachers, healthcare workers, or municipal employees, who see union membership as an important protection of workers' rights.

Younger adults and those in precarious or informal employment who have never been union members, either because their work arrangements don't facilitate it or because they feel unions are irrelevant to their situation.
Small business owners, artisans, or professionals who have never been union members and identify more with employer associations or professional orders than with worker unions.
Practicing Catholic who maintains a strong connection to the Church, attends mass regularly, and considers religious identity a core part of their Belgian cultural heritage.
Nominally Catholic or Christian who was raised in a religious household and still identifies with a denomination culturally, even if they rarely attend services or practice actively.
Secular liberal who does not identify with any religion, supports LGBT rights strongly, and sees religion as a private or irrelevant matter in modern Belgian society.
Muslim or member of another minority religion, particularly from immigrant communities in cities like Brussels or Antwerp, who maintains a strong religious identity.
Agnostic or atheist who was raised without strong religious ties and firmly does not consider themselves part of any religious denomination.
Socially conservative Russians who hold traditional values and would genuinely feel ashamed if a close family member were gay or lesbian, seeing it as a source of family dishonor and social stigma.
Moderately traditional Russians who feel uncomfortable with homosexuality in their own family but wouldn't strongly identify with shame, leaning toward agreement but with some ambivalence.
Ambivalent Russians who are caught between traditional upbringing and more modern exposure, neither fully agreeing nor disagreeing, unsure how they would actually feel in such a situation.
Tolerant Russians who, despite living in a conservative society, believe gay people should live freely and would not feel ashamed of a gay family member, disagreeing with the statement.
Strongly liberal or younger Russians who firmly reject the idea of shame associated with a gay family member and would actively support and accept them, disagreeing strongly with the statement.
Devout Catholic who actively practices their faith and strongly identifies with the Catholic Church, seeing religion as central to Polish identity and daily life.
Nominally religious Pole who identifies as Catholic by tradition and cultural heritage but does not practice regularly or hold strong religious convictions.
Secular-leaning individual who has drifted away from religious identification, perhaps due to disillusionment with the Church's role in politics or personal skepticism.
Convinced non-believer or atheist who explicitly rejects religious affiliation and sees themselves as secular, possibly influenced by education or urban living.
Person belonging to a minority religion or denomination (such as Orthodox Christianity, Protestantism, or another faith), who identifies with their specific religious community.

Older, religiously observant Irish person with limited formal education who is not politically active and has never signed a petition, seeing it as something other people do rather than a meaningful way to make change.
Middle-aged Irish person who occasionally engages with community issues and has signed a petition once or twice, perhaps on a local matter or something shared on social media.
Younger Irish person with low formal education but some social awareness, who has signed an online petition in the past year, finding it an easy and accessible form of civic participation.
Socially conservative, religiously devout Irish person who distrusts petitions and political activism generally, preferring to leave matters to elected representatives or the Church.
Engaged community member who has signed multiple petitions on issues like local services or social causes, seeing petitions as a straightforward way to have their voice heard.
Socially liberal older Belgians who strongly support LGBT rights and would feel no shame whatsoever about a gay family member, viewing it as a normal part of life.

Moderate, tolerant older Belgians who believe gay people should live freely but still carry some residual cultural discomfort, and would disagree with feeling ashamed without being strongly opposed to it.
Religious older Belgians who hold traditional Catholic values and feel some degree of shame or embarrassment about having a gay close family member, though they may not express it harshly.
Ambivalent older Belgians who are caught between traditional upbringing and modern norms, neither agreeing nor disagreeing with feeling ashamed, reflecting genuine internal conflict.
Strongly traditional older Belgians who openly agree they would feel ashamed, rooted in deep religious or conservative cultural convictions about family and sexuality.

Politically disengaged retirees who have largely withdrawn from civic life and rarely participate in formal political actions like petitions, feeling that such activities are for younger or more politically active people.

Civic-minded older Swiss citizens who occasionally engage with petitions when a local or national issue strongly affects them, seeing it as a legitimate and accessible form of democratic participation.
Traditionally conservative older Swiss who are skeptical of petitions as an effective tool and prefer established institutional channels, rarely signing them.
Actively engaged older citizens who participate in various civic activities including petitions, often connected to community organizations, environmental causes, or political parties.
Older Swiss who have signed petitions specifically around issues directly relevant to their age group, such as pension reform or healthcare, but otherwise do not engage in civic activism.
Devout Catholic middle-aged Poles who were raised in a religious household and continue to identify strongly with the Catholic Church as a core part of their Polish identity and daily life.
Culturally Catholic Poles who identify with Catholicism as part of their heritage and national identity, even if they do not practice regularly or hold deep personal faith.
Secular or non-religious Poles who grew up during the communist era and retained a skeptical or indifferent attitude toward organized religion, not identifying with any denomination.
Poles who belong to minority religious denominations such as Orthodox Christianity or Protestantism, identifying with their specific faith community as distinct from the Catholic majority.
Agnostic or atheist Poles who actively reject religious identification, often educated urban individuals who see religion as incompatible with their worldview.

Socially liberal urban Russians, often younger and educated, who strongly disagree that they would feel ashamed of a gay family member and see sexual orientation as a personal matter deserving acceptance.
Moderate Russians who disagree with feeling ashamed but hold this view somewhat quietly, accepting gay relatives without enthusiasm while not making it a point of pride or conflict.
Ambivalent or conflict-avoidant Russians who neither agree nor disagree, feeling genuinely torn between traditional social expectations and personal loyalty to family members.
Traditionally minded Russians, often older or more religious, who would agree they feel ashamed, viewing homosexuality as a moral failing or social stigma that reflects on the family.

Strongly conservative Russians, often influenced by Orthodox Christian values or nationalist sentiment, who strongly agree they would feel ashamed and see homosexuality as deeply incompatible with Russian family values.

Traditionally-minded married Austrians who view marriage as the proper foundation for cohabitation and disapprove of couples living together outside of wedlock, seeing it as undermining family values.
Neutral or ambivalent married Austrians who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, viewing it as a personal choice that doesn't particularly concern them.
Pragmatic married Austrians who approve of cohabitation as a reasonable step before or instead of marriage, possibly having lived with their partner before marrying themselves.
Strongly liberal married Austrians who enthusiastically approve of cohabitation without marriage, seeing it as a fully valid lifestyle choice equal to marriage.
Religiously or culturally conservative married Austrians who strongly disapprove of living together outside of marriage, viewing it as morally wrong and socially harmful.

Older workers or retirees who were part of Italy's strong union culture during their working years, particularly in manufacturing or public sectors, and are now former members who valued collective bargaining.
Middle-aged employed individuals in stable jobs who have never joined a union, either because their sector is not heavily unionized or because they see unions as ineffective or politically biased.
Younger workers or those in precarious employment (part-time, temporary contracts) who have never been union members, as their work arrangements make union membership less accessible or relevant.

Current union members, typically in public administration, education, or large industrial firms, who see union membership as important for protecting workers' rights and wages in Italy's challenging economic climate.
Self-employed individuals or small business owners who have never been part of a trade union, as their work status makes union membership inapplicable or unappealing.
Politically passive working-class Russians who focus on day-to-day survival and have never considered boycotting products as a form of civic action, seeing it as irrelevant to their lives.
Older, Soviet-era Russians who are unfamiliar with the concept of consumer boycotts as political tools and simply buy what is available and affordable.
Younger, more educated urban Russians who are aware of boycotts as a concept but have not personally participated in one in the last 12 months.
Patriotically motivated Russians who may have participated in informal boycotts of Western goods following sanctions and counter-sanctions around 2014-2016, seeing it as supporting their country.
Politically engaged or liberal-leaning Russians who have consciously boycotted certain products for ethical, environmental, or political reasons.

Secular, urban French adults in their 50s-60s who came of age after May 1968 and embraced cohabitation as a normal part of adult life; they have almost certainly lived with a partner before marriage or instead of it.
Moderately traditional French adults who cohabited briefly before eventually marrying, reflecting the widespread normalization of trial cohabitation in France from the 1970s-1980s onward.
Lifelong unmarried cohabitants who never formalized their relationship through marriage or civil union, a lifestyle that became increasingly common in France and which this age group helped pioneer.

Traditionally or religiously oriented French adults, often Catholic, who married without prior cohabitation and view marriage as the proper foundation for living together; they have not lived with a partner outside of marriage.

Divorced or separated individuals who, after the end of their marriage, entered into a new cohabiting relationship without remarrying, giving them experience of living with a partner outside formal union.
Secular-minded Belgian women who have drifted away from religion over generations and do not identify with any religious denomination, seeing themselves as non-religious or atheist.
Nominally Catholic women who were raised in the Catholic tradition and still identify culturally with Catholicism, even if they rarely attend church or practice actively.
Practicing Catholic women who actively participate in church life and strongly identify with their Catholic faith as a core part of their identity.
Women from immigrant or minority backgrounds who identify with Islam or another non-Christian religion, maintaining a strong religious identity tied to their community and heritage.
Agnostic or spiritually curious women who do not align with any organized religion or denomination but may hold personal spiritual beliefs, choosing 'No' when asked about belonging to a religion.
Younger, urban, never-married Bulgarians who have themselves cohabited or are open to it, and who fully approve of living together without marriage as a modern and practical choice.
Moderately liberal Bulgarians who lean toward approval of cohabitation but with some reservations, seeing it as acceptable though perhaps not ideal compared to marriage.
Neutral or ambivalent individuals who neither approve nor disapprove, viewing cohabitation as a personal matter they have no strong feelings about either way.
Traditionally minded Bulgarians, often influenced by Orthodox Christian values or older cultural norms, who disapprove of living together outside of marriage as improper or morally wrong.
Strongly conservative individuals who firmly disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, seeing it as a serious breach of family and religious values.
Working-age employed individuals who focus on their jobs and family life, with little time or inclination to participate in voluntary organisations or associations beyond their immediate circle.
Retired or older individuals living on pensions who may have more time but limited energy or motivation to engage in organisational work, preferring passive civic engagement if any.
Community-minded individuals, often middle-class professionals or those with higher education, who actively volunteer or work within local charities, sports clubs, or civic associations.
Younger adults or students who occasionally get involved in university societies, community groups, or activist organisations, though participation can be sporadic.
Individuals facing financial difficulty or precarious employment who are too preoccupied with making ends meet to dedicate time to working in organisations or associations.
Young or middle-aged urban Finns who embraced cohabitation as a normal life stage before or instead of marriage, reflecting Finland's high rates of consensual unions.
Older Finns or those from more traditional backgrounds who married early and never lived with a partner outside of marriage, viewing marriage as the proper framework for partnership.
Finns who cohabited with a partner at some point in their lives but eventually married or separated, representing a transitional phase common in Finnish relationship patterns.
Younger Finns who are currently single or in early relationships and have not yet had the opportunity to cohabit with a partner, though they generally view cohabitation positively.
Finns with strong religious or conservative values who deliberately chose not to cohabit before marriage, seeing marriage as the appropriate precondition for living together.
Socially liberal Czech women who strongly support LGBT rights and would feel no shame whatsoever if a close family member were gay or lesbian, viewing it as a completely normal part of life.
Moderate, tolerant Czech women who broadly support LGBT freedoms but may feel mild discomfort or uncertainty about a gay family member, though they would not describe it as shame.
Ambivalent Czech women who neither strongly support nor oppose LGBT rights and would feel genuinely conflicted or neutral if a close family member came out, unsure how to feel.

Traditionally minded Czech women who hold conservative social values and would feel some degree of shame or embarrassment if a close family member were gay or lesbian, though they might not openly express it.

Strongly traditional or religious Czech women who hold firm conservative views on sexuality and would feel definite shame if a close family member were gay or lesbian, seeing it as contrary to their values.
Socially conservative older Germans with traditional values who believe marriage and adoption are institutions reserved for heterosexual couples, often influenced by religious or cultural upbringing.

Pragmatic middle-ground individuals who are not strongly opposed to gay rights but feel uncertain about adoption specifically, preferring to neither strongly agree nor disagree on this sensitive topic.
Younger or more open-minded workers who broadly support equal rights for LGBT couples including adoption, seeing it as a matter of fairness and non-discrimination.
Strongly traditionalist individuals, often with restrictive views on immigration as well, who firmly disagree with same-sex adoption and see it as contrary to natural family structures.

Moderate supporters who agree that gay and lesbian couples should have adoption rights but without strong conviction, reflecting a general live-and-let-live attitude common in urban or younger demographics.
Dual-income married couples with stable wage employment who feel financially secure and comfortable, able to cover expenses and save without stress.
Middle-income married households, often with one primary earner on wages or salary, who manage their bills and expenses adequately but without much surplus.
Self-employed or farming households with variable income who generally cope but feel some financial uncertainty depending on the season or market conditions.
Households relying partly on pensions, benefits, or lower wages who find it genuinely difficult to make ends meet each month.
Households in serious financial hardship, possibly dealing with unemployment or very low income, who find their present income very difficult to live on.
Older, less digitally engaged Italians who rarely or never use the internet, often retired or in manual occupations, who see the internet as unnecessary or too complicated for their daily lives.
Middle-aged Italians with moderate digital engagement who use the internet a few times a week, primarily for email, news, or occasional shopping, but do not feel compelled to be online constantly.
Working-age Italians who use the internet most days for a mix of work and personal purposes, comfortable with technology but not fully immersed in a digital lifestyle.
Younger and professionally active Italians who use the internet every day across multiple devices, integrating it seamlessly into both their work and social lives.
Italians of various ages who use the internet only occasionally, perhaps for specific tasks like banking or looking up information, but who otherwise prefer offline activities and interactions.

Middle-aged or older Dutch adults with lower secondary education who grew up in an era when cohabitation was becoming normalized; they have lived with a partner before marriage or instead of marriage, reflecting the broadly permissive Dutch attitude toward cohabitation.
Younger adults in this education group who are currently in or have recently been in a cohabiting relationship, seeing it as a normal step before or instead of marriage in contemporary Dutch society.
Adults who married relatively young or directly without cohabiting first, often influenced by more traditional or religious family values, and have never lived with a partner outside of marriage.
Older individuals in this group who came of age when cohabitation was less socially accepted and who followed more traditional paths, never having lived with a partner without being married.
Single or divorced individuals who have had various living arrangements but never specifically cohabited with a partner outside of a formal union, either due to circumstance or personal choice.
Working-age employed men who are focused on their jobs and family life, with little time or inclination for civic organizations or associations beyond their immediate responsibilities.
Older or retired men who grew up in communist Poland with a distrust of organized collective activity, and who remain disengaged from voluntary associations in the post-communist era.
Religiously active Catholic men who participate in church-affiliated organizations or parish associations, counting this as working within an organization.
Civic-minded men, often younger and more educated, who are actively involved in NGOs, community groups, sports clubs, or professional associations and see such participation as important.
Men involved in trade unions, political party structures, or professional guilds, particularly in industrial or public-sector workplaces, who regularly work within formal organizations.

Politically disengaged centrists who feel no strong attachment to any party, reflecting the broader French disillusionment with traditional political structures and the rise of 'ni gauche ni droite' sentiment after Macron's 2017 election.

Left-leaning workers or union members who feel a clear affinity with parties like La France Insoumise or the Parti Socialiste, maintaining a traditional partisan identity rooted in class and labor solidarity.
Right or center-right oriented individuals who identify with Les Républicains or the Rassemblement National, feeling a clear partisan home despite the fragmentation of the French right.

Macron supporters who feel close to La République En Marche, a newer partisan identity that emerged from the 2017 political realignment and appeals to educated, urban, moderate voters in this age group.

Cynical or apolitical individuals who have actively rejected all parties, distrustful of the entire political class and unwilling to identify with any organization regardless of their personal values.
Progressive Icelanders who strongly support LGBT rights and feel no shame whatsoever about having a gay or lesbian family member, viewing such feelings of shame as outdated and discriminatory.
Socially liberal Icelanders who are comfortable with LGBT family members and would disagree with feeling ashamed, though they may not feel as strongly or vocally about it.
Neutral or uncertain Icelanders who have mixed feelings, perhaps due to older cultural or religious influences, but would not strongly endorse shame either.
Traditionally minded Icelanders, often older or more religious, who retain some discomfort with homosexuality in their family and might mildly agree with feeling some shame.

Strongly traditional or religious Icelanders who would genuinely feel ashamed if a close family member were gay or lesbian, holding conservative views that conflict with mainstream Icelandic attitudes.

Fully retired individuals with no professional obligations who see no reason to take work-related courses or attend professional conferences, as they have left the workforce entirely and focus on leisure and family.

Recently retired people who occasionally attend lectures or cultural conferences out of personal interest but do not consider them work-related, and thus would answer no to this specific question about work improvement.

Semi-retired or partially active professionals who still maintain some work activity or consulting role and have attended at least one course or conference in the past year to keep their skills current.

Retired individuals with a strong interest in lifelong learning who actively seek out courses and lectures, sometimes through senior universities or community programs, and interpret the question broadly enough to answer yes.
Retired people who would have liked to attend professional development activities but faced barriers such as health issues, limited mobility, or lack of access to relevant programs in their area.

Traditional older Bulgarians who hold conservative family values and believe children should only be born within marriage; they disapprove of having children outside of wedlock as it goes against their religious and cultural upbringing.

Moderately traditional Bulgarians who are somewhat uncomfortable with having children outside marriage but recognize it as increasingly common; they lean toward disapproval but are not strongly opposed.
Neutral middle-ground Bulgarians who neither approve nor disapprove, seeing it as a personal choice that does not concern them, even if it differs from their own preferences or lifestyle.

Pragmatic younger or urban Bulgarians who accept cohabitation and family formation outside marriage as a normal modern lifestyle choice, approving of couples who have children together even without formal marriage.
Strongly liberal Bulgarians, often younger and more educated, who fully embrace non-traditional family structures and strongly approve of having children with a partner regardless of marital status.

A woman raised in a traditional Polish household where her mother was a full-time homemaker, which was very common in communist and post-communist Poland, especially in rural or working-class families.

A woman whose mother worked as an employee, likely in a state enterprise, public sector, or factory, reflecting the high female labor force participation encouraged during the communist era in Poland.
A woman whose mother was self-employed or ran a small family business, a less common but present situation particularly in small trade or farming communities.
A woman who grew up on a farm where her mother worked in agriculture, which may not fit neatly into employee or self-employed categories and reflects Poland's significant rural population.
A woman whose mother was absent or deceased during her childhood, leaving her without a maternal figure in the household at age 14.

Young to middle-aged employed professionals who use the internet daily for both work tasks and personal activities like social media, news, and entertainment, seeing it as an indispensable part of modern life.
Office and administrative workers who use the internet most days for work-related purposes and regularly browse at home, but don't feel compelled to be online every single day.

Older employed workers in manual or trade occupations who use the internet only a few times a week, mainly for practical purposes like checking email or looking up information, but don't rely on it heavily.
Workers in their 50s or older who are less comfortable with technology and only occasionally go online, perhaps to check messages or use a specific service, but largely manage without it.
Older or rural workers who have little interest or access to the internet and rarely or never use it, relying on traditional media and face-to-face communication instead.

Older workers or retirees who were employed in traditional industries like manufacturing or public services, where union membership was common; they were members in the past but have since retired or left those sectors.
Middle-aged employed individuals in stable jobs who have never joined a union, either because their workplace doesn't have one or because they see little personal benefit; they have no union history.
Current union members, typically employed in public sector or large companies, who see the union as important for protecting their wages and working conditions.
Younger or lower-educated workers in precarious, part-time, or informal employment who have never had the opportunity or incentive to join a union.
Homemakers, unemployed individuals, or those outside the formal labor market who have never been in a position to join a trade union and have no connection to organized labor.

Fidesz loyalists who strongly identify with Viktor Orbán's party and feel a clear partisan attachment, seeing Fidesz as the natural home for patriotic Hungarians concerned about national sovereignty and economic stability.

Opposition-leaning voters who identify with one of the fragmented left-wing or liberal parties such as MSZP, DK, or Momentum, feeling a clear but sometimes reluctant partisan attachment as a counterweight to Fidesz dominance.

Politically disengaged working-class individuals who are coping financially and feel that no party truly represents their interests, expressing no particular party affiliation and general cynicism toward the political establishment.

Soft independents who lean toward a party but do not feel strongly attached, often shifting between options or abstaining, and who answer 'no' because their connection to any party feels too weak to call it a real closeness.

Younger professionals and educated urbanites who are politically aware but deliberately reject partisan identity, valuing independence and distrusting all parties equally in a polarized political environment.
